historical_timeline.summary: Measles, with a long recovery and a year in bed.
Cholera, with lingering asthma and digestive problems.
Translation of Menabrea's article on the Analytical Engine, with her Notes.
Declining health; several medicines; laudanum and opium.
Gambling on horses and pawned jewels.
Wracked with pain as the cancer advanced.
Died in Marylebone, London; owed about 2,000 pounds in gambling debts.

claims.statement: Augusta Ada Byron was born on December 10, 1815, in Piccadilly, London, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron and Anne Isabella Byron.

born in Piccadilly, Middlesex (now in London)

claims.statement: She was often ill as a child. In 1829, at 13, she caught measles, from which she took a long while to recover; she was bedridden for a whole year.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented childhood illness. The brief's 'unable to walk' and later crutches were not found in a fetched source and are not recorded.

source_links.locator: 1829, measles, a long recovery

claims.statement: On July 8, 1835, she married William King, who was created an earl in 1838, making her Countess of Lovelace.

source_links.locator: married on 8 July 1835

claims.statement: Her health suffered after a bout of cholera in 1837, and she had lingering problems with asthma and her digestive system.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented in a general biography only.

claims.statement: Her doctors gave her painkillers such as laudanum and opium; she reportedly had mood swings and hallucinations.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented in a general biography only; no doses or dates are given. Anchors the modern history of long-term prescribed opium tincture; no substance use disorder is inferred.

claims.statement: Between 1842 and 1843 she translated L. F. Menabrea's article on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and added her own extensive Notes, published in 1843 under the initials A.A.L. The Notes, which include a method for computing Bernoulli numbers on the engine, are often described as the first published computer program.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her mathematical work; anchors the modern goal of clear-headed working hours.

claims.statement: Her health, always fragile, declined sharply after 1843. By the end of that year she was taking several medicines for different health problems; in 1844 she wrote that a recent illness had left her 'utterly unable to think even of my studies', and she thought of writing a scientific study of the effects of opium and wine based on her own experience. In the 1840s she had what she called heart or rheumatic attacks.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented chronic ill health and her own use of opium; no diagnosis is inferred.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care, gynecologic oncology and early palliative care for a 35-year-old mathematician with five months of abnormal bleeding and pelvic pain who has taken prescribed opium tincture for years: speculum examination and biopsy of a visible cervical tumor at the first visit, with tumor HPV typing; intravenous iron for iron deficiency anemia from blood loss; conversion of an unmeasured opium tincture to measured oral morphine, then long-acting morphine, with naloxone, a bowel regimen, safe storage and a prescription monitoring check, applying the ASCO 1848 guideline on opioids for cancer pain and noting that the CDC 1847 opioid guideline does not cover cancer pain; FIGO 1843 staging with MRI and PET-CT and biopsy of a lung metastasis (stage IVB); tumor biomarkers (PD-L1, mismatch repair, HER2) and why germline testing is not indicated; palliative pelvic radiation for bleeding; first-line carboplatin, paclitaxel and pembrolizumab under the NCCN cervical cancer guideline and KEYNOTE-826, without bevacizumab while she was bleeding after pelvic radiation; specialist palliative care from diagnosis (ASCO 1849); immune-related thyroid monitoring; opioid-induced constipation; goals-of-care conversations and advance care planning; vaccination of an adult on chemotherapy; and protecting clear-headed hours for her mathematical work.

visit_schedule.purpose: New patient visit for abnormal bleeding and pelvic pain: history, speculum examination and cervical biopsy, blood count and iron studies, conversion of opium tincture to measured oral morphine, an iron infusion, and a gynecologic oncology referral
Two-week follow-up and gynecologic oncology consultation: pathology, MRI and PET-CT, staging, treatment intent, palliative care, and long-acting morphine
Six-week review: bleeding and pain after palliative pelvic radiation, the first cycle of chemotherapy with pembrolizumab, blood counts, mood and opioid safety
Fourteen-week review: restaging CT, blood counts, iron and thyroid, pain, and a goals-of-care conversation
Twenty-week review after the last chemotherapy cycle: blood counts, thyroid on pembrolizumab, tapering morphine, mood and her work

consultant_note.history: Mrs. Lovelace, a 35-year-old mathematician, is seen at the request of Dr. Whitley-Adeyemi for a cervical mass found two weeks ago after five months of abnormal bleeding and pelvic pain. The bleeding is lighter since the first iron infusion but continues. Her pain averages 6 of 10 on oral morphine solution 5 mg about six times a day, without drowsiness; she stopped the opium tincture she had taken for two years. She has no cough, hemoptysis, bone pain, leg swelling, or urinary or bowel symptoms beyond opioid-related constipation. She has never had cervical screening. She does not wish to preserve fertility. She asked to be told the findings directly
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Cervical biopsy: invasive adenocarcinoma, usual (HPV-associated) type, p16 diffusely positive, HPV 18 detected; PD-L1 combined positive score 5; mismatch repair proteins retained; HER2 immunohistochemistry 1+. Pelvic MRI a week ago: 5.2 cm endocervical tumor with left parametrial invasion, not reaching the sidewall, no hydronephrosis, an enlarged left external iliac node. FDG PET-CT five days ago: avid tumor, avid left pelvic and para-aortic nodes, six avid nodules in both lungs up to 1.4 cm, no bone or liver lesions. assessment.assessment: The lung nodules and para-aortic nodes on PET-CT mean distant spread, stage IVB by imaging; because this decides that treatment is palliative rather than curative, a lung nodule should be biopsied to confirm it before systemic therapy. With PD-L1 combined positive score 5, the NCCN preferred first-line treatment is carboplatin or cisplatin with paclitaxel and pembrolizumab, with or without bevacizumab, based on KEYNOTE-826. I recommend carboplatin, for ease and less toxicity, and leaving out bevacizumab for now, because she is bleeding from the tumor and will have pelvic radiation, which raise the risks of hemorrhage and fistula. Cervical cancer is not part of a hereditary cancer syndrome, so germline testing is not indicated; the tumor biomarkers are complete for first-line and later choices
